items.title: Core Principles & the Evolution of Indian Foreign Policy
items.body:
### Core principles and how foreign policy evolved

**In one line**
India's foreign policy is the set of guiding ideas (Panchsheel, non-alignment, strategic autonomy) that decide how India deals with other countries, and it has shifted from idealism in 1947 to pragmatic multi-alignment today.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC/UPSC repeatedly test the founding principles, their dates and framers, and the correct name for the modern posture. Students confuse 'non-alignment' with 'neutrality' and mix up Panchsheel's partner country.

**The story (cause → what happened → result)**
After 1947 a newly free, poor India did not want to be dragged into the US-versus-USSR Cold War, so Nehru chose **non-alignment** — judging each issue on merit instead of joining a bloc. In 1954 India and China signed an agreement on trade with the Tibet region that spelt out **Panchsheel**, the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence. The **first NAM summit** met at **Belgrade in 1961**. The 1962 war with China and the 1971 treaty with the USSR pushed India toward realism; after the 1991 economic reforms foreign policy became an engine for trade and investment; and from about 2014 India openly follows **multi-alignment / strategic autonomy** — working with many powers at once without joining anyone's camp.

**Picture it (timeline)**

| Phase | Years | Keynote |
|---|---|---|
| Nehruvian idealism & non-alignment | 1947–64 | Panchsheel, NAM, moral voice |
| Realism | 1962–1991 | 1962 war, 1971 Indo-Soviet Treaty |
| Economic diplomacy | post-1991 | Reforms, markets, Look East |
| Multi-alignment | post-2014 | Quad + BRICS/SCO at the same time |

**Terms explained**
- **Panchsheel** — the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence (mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, mutual non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, peaceful coexistence).
- **Non-Alignment (NAM)** — refusing to join either Cold-War military bloc; it means independent judgement, not passivity or neutrality.
- **Strategic autonomy / multi-alignment** — keeping independent decision-making while partnering with several powers issue-by-issue.
- **Determinants** — the factors that shape policy: geography (long coastline, Himalayan frontiers), history and anti-colonial values, economic needs (energy, markets), national capability (military/nuclear), domestic politics, and the international system. Foreign affairs is a **Union executive** function (Union List entries 10–14).

**Don't confuse**
- Non-alignment is **not** neutrality or isolation — India took clear positions (e.g. against apartheid).
- Panchsheel (1954) was with **China**, not the USSR (the 1971 treaty) or Nepal (the 1950 treaty).

**Remember it**
'**Belgrade 1961**, Panchsheel is **China 1954**' — two dates that unlock most NAM questions.

**TL;DR**
- Panchsheel = Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, from the 1954 India–China Tibet agreement.
- NAM's first summit was at Belgrade in 1961; founders included Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno, Nkrumah.
- Strategic autonomy = independent decision-making while engaging multiple powers.
- Evolution: idealism → post-1962/1971 realism → post-1991 economic diplomacy → post-2014 multi-alignment.
- Foreign affairs is a Union executive function (Union List entries 10–14).
keyPoints: Panchsheel = Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, from the 1954 India-China Tibet agreement.
NAM's first summit was at Belgrade in 1961; founders included Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno, Nkrumah.
Strategic autonomy = independent decision-making while engaging multiple powers (multi-alignment).
Evolution: Nehruvian idealism -> post-1962/1971 realism -> post-1991 economic diplomacy -> post-2014 multi-alignment.
Determinants: geography, history/values, economic needs, national capability, domestic politics, international system.

items.title: Neighbourhood First, Gujral Doctrine, Act East & SAGAR
items.body:
### India's named regional policies

**In one line**
These are the branded policies India uses for its neighbourhood and the wider region — Gujral Doctrine, Neighbourhood First, Act East and SAGAR — each with a year and a focus the exam loves to match.

**Why it is asked**
Match-the-following questions pair the policy with its focus, and statement questions test the year and the idea (e.g. 'non-reciprocity', 'Look East became Act East in 2014').

**The story (cause → what happened → result)**
As the largest country in South Asia, India realised that strict give-and-take with much smaller neighbours bred resentment, so in **1996 the Gujral Doctrine** offered **non-reciprocity** — unilateral concessions to smaller neighbours (not Pakistan) to build trust. In **2014** this matured into **Neighbourhood First**. The **Look East** policy of **1991** (opening to Southeast Asia for trade) was upgraded in **2014** to **Act East**, adding strategy, security and connectivity and reaching East Asia and the Indo-Pacific. In **2015** India gave its Indian Ocean maritime vision a name — **SAGAR**.

**Picture it (policy → year → focus)**

| Policy / Vision | Year | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| **Gujral Doctrine** | 1996 | Non-reciprocity — unilateral concessions to smaller neighbours (not Pakistan) |
| **Neighbourhood First** | 2014 | Priority to immediate South Asian neighbours; connectivity, aid, 'first responder' role |
| **Act East** | 2014 (from Look East, 1991) | ASEAN, East Asia and the Indo-Pacific — Culture, Commerce, Connectivity, Capacity |
| **SAGAR** | 2015 | 'Security And Growth for All in the Region' — Indian Ocean |

**Terms explained**
- **Non-reciprocity** — giving a benefit without demanding an equal return, to build goodwill.
- **SAGAR** — 'Security And Growth for All in the Region', India's Indian-Ocean maritime doctrine.
- **Net security provider / first responder** — India supplies security and is first to help in a crisis in the Indian Ocean Region (e.g. Vaccine Maitri, disaster-relief or HADR missions).

**Neighbours snapshot (as of Oct 2026)**
*Bhutan* — closest partner, hydropower ties; *Nepal* — 1950 Treaty, open border, periodic friction over boundary maps; *Bangladesh* — an interim government under **Muhammad Yunus** took charge after the August 2024 change of government, with a general election due in 2026, and ties cooled in that period; *Sri Lanka* — economic-recovery support after the 2022 crisis; *Maldives* — recalibration after an initial 'India Out' phase; *Myanmar* — engagement despite post-coup instability; *Pakistan* — near-frozen ties, worsened by the 2025 Pahalgam attack.

**Don't confuse**
- **SAGAR** (maritime, Indian Ocean) vs **Neighbourhood First** (land neighbours) — the exam swaps these.
- Act East (2014) is the upgrade of **Look East (1991)**, not a brand-new 2014 idea.

**Remember it**
'**Gujral gives, SAGAR sails**' — Gujral = unilateral giving; SAGAR = the sea/Indian Ocean.

**TL;DR**
- Gujral Doctrine (1996) = non-reciprocity toward smaller neighbours (excludes Pakistan).
- Neighbourhood First (2014) prioritises immediate South Asian neighbours.
- Act East (2014) grew from Look East (1991); reaches ASEAN and the Indo-Pacific.
- SAGAR (2015) = 'Security and Growth for All in the Region' — Indian Ocean vision.
- Bangladesh: interim government under Muhammad Yunus after Aug 2024, election due 2026.
keyPoints: Gujral Doctrine (1996) = non-reciprocity toward smaller neighbours (excludes Pakistan).
Neighbourhood First (2014) prioritises immediate South Asian neighbours.
Act East (2014) grew from Look East (1991); reaches ASEAN and the Indo-Pacific.
SAGAR (2015) = 'Security and Growth for All in the Region' — Indian Ocean maritime vision.
Bangladesh: interim government under Muhammad Yunus after Aug 2024 change; general election due 2026.
India brands itself a 'net security provider' and 'first responder' in the IOR.

items.title: Relations with Major Powers — US, Russia, China, Pakistan
items.body:
### India and the big four relationships

**In one line**
How India manages its four most exam-relevant relationships — the United States, Russia, China and Pakistan — each with its own label, agreements and flashpoints.

**Why it is asked**
Questions test the exact name of each partnership, the defence agreements (LEMOA/COMCASA/BECA), and recent events (Galwan 2020, the October 2024 patrolling pact, Operation Sindoor 2025).

**The story (cause → what happened → result)**
After the Cold War India drew closer to the **United States**; shared concern about China and a booming tech relationship produced a 'Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership', three foundational defence agreements and, in 2023, the technology initiative **iCET**. With **Russia**, the Soviet-era friendship survived as a 'Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership' built on weapons, nuclear power and, since 2022, cheap oil. With **China**, trade and shared forums coexist with rivalry on an undemarcated border: the **Galwan clash (June 2020)** was the first deadly India-China fighting since 1975, and an **October 2024 patrolling agreement** for eastern Ladakh let the two leaders meet at the Kazan BRICS summit. With **Pakistan**, cross-border terrorism keeps ties near-frozen; after the **April 2025 Pahalgam attack** India launched **Operation Sindoor (May 2025)** and held the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance.

**Picture it (partner → label → anchors)**

| Partner | Label | Anchors / flashpoints |
|---|---|---|
| USA | Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership | LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA; iCET (2023); Quad |
| Russia | Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership | S-400, BrahMos, Kudankulam; discounted crude since 2022 |
| China | Rival-partner across the LAC | Galwan 2020; Oct 2024 patrolling pact (Depsang, Demchok) |
| Pakistan | Near-frozen | Pahalgam 2025 → Operation Sindoor; IWT in abeyance |

**Terms explained**
- **LEMOA / COMCASA / BECA** — the three 'foundational' India–US defence agreements covering logistics sharing, secure communications and geospatial data.
- **iCET** — Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (2023): AI, semiconductors, space, quantum, defence tech.
- **LAC (Line of Actual Control)** — the notional, un-demarcated India–China line, perceived differently by each side — not a settled boundary.
- **Indus Waters Treaty (1960)** — the India–Pakistan river-sharing treaty, held 'in abeyance' by India after Pahalgam.

**Don't confuse**
- **LAC** (India–China, undemarcated) vs the **LoC** (India–Pakistan line in Kashmir).
- The India–US ties are a 'partnership', **not** a treaty military alliance — India still buys Russian S-400.

**Remember it**
'**L-C-B with the US, S-400 with Russia**' — the Western pacts are letters, the Russian link is hardware.

**TL;DR**
- India–US foundational pacts: LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA; tech via iCET (2023).
- India–Russia = 'Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership'; S-400, BrahMos, Kudankulam, discounted oil.
- LAC is undemarcated; Galwan clash was June 2020 (first fatal since 1975).
- Oct 2024 India–China patrolling pact (Depsang, Demchok) preceded a Modi–Xi meeting at Kazan.
- Operation Sindoor (May 2025) followed the Pahalgam attack (April 2025); Indus Waters Treaty held in abeyance.
keyPoints: India-US foundational pacts: LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA; tech via iCET (2023).
India-Russia = 'Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership'; S-400, BrahMos, Kudankulam, discounted oil.
LAC is undemarcated; Galwan clash was June 2020 (first fatal since 1975).
Oct 2024 India-China patrolling pact (Depsang, Demchok) preceded a Modi-Xi meeting at Kazan.
Operation Sindoor (May 2025) followed the Pahalgam attack (April 2025); Indus Waters Treaty held in abeyance.

items.title: Key Groupings — Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20
items.body:
### The groupings India sits in

**In one line**
India practises multi-alignment — belonging at the same time to Western-leaning groupings (Quad, G20) and Eurasian ones (BRICS, SCO), which is why it keeps independent judgement.

**Why it is asked**
The exam tests membership (who is in, who is not), the correct nature of each body (dialogue vs alliance), and the latest facts (BRICS expansion, G20's African Union, SCO membership year).

**The story (cause → what happened → result)**
To hedge in a multipolar world India joined groupings across the spectrum. The **Quad** (with the US, Japan, Australia) is a diplomatic forum for a free and open Indo-Pacific — revived in 2017 and raised to leaders' summits from 2021. **BRICS** grew from five to **ten members** after the 2024–25 expansion. In the **SCO** India has been a **full member since 2017**. In the **G20**, under India's **2023 presidency**, the **African Union** was admitted as a permanent member, strengthening the 'Voice of the Global South'.

**Picture it (grouping → members → India's role)**

| Grouping | Members / status | India's role |
|---|---|---|
| **Quad** | India, US, Japan, Australia | Diplomatic forum (not a military alliance); revived 2017, summits from 2021 |
| **BRICS** | 10 (2025): Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa + Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE, Indonesia | NDB and Contingent Reserve Arrangement; India chairs the 2026 summit |
| **SCO** | China, Russia, Central Asian states, India, Pakistan, Iran | Full member since 2017; counter-terror via RATS; chaired 2023 |
| **G20** | 19 countries + EU + African Union | 2023 presidency admitted the AU; 'Voice of the Global South' |

**Terms explained**
- **NDB (New Development Bank)** — the BRICS bank, headquartered in **Shanghai**.
- **Contingent Reserve Arrangement** — a BRICS pool of currency reserves for members in balance-of-payments trouble.
- **RATS** — the SCO's Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure.
- **Global South** — developing countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America whose interests India champions.

**Don't confuse**
- The **Quad is a dialogue**, not a NATO-style treaty alliance — India rejects that framing.
- BRICS **Indonesia** joined as a full member (January 2025); **Saudi Arabia** was invited but has not formally joined.

**Remember it**
'**Quad + BRICS at once**' is the one-line proof of multi-alignment; 'BRICS went **5 → 10**'.

**TL;DR**
- Quad (India, US, Japan, Australia) is a strategic dialogue, not a treaty alliance; revived 2017.
- BRICS has 10 members from 2025 (added Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE, Indonesia); India chairs the 2026 summit.
- India joined the SCO as a full member in 2017; its counter-terror arm is RATS.
- G20 = 19 countries + EU + African Union (AU added at India's 2023 New Delhi presidency).
- India also engages via I2U2, BIMSTEC and IBSA, and champions the Global South.
keyPoints: Quad (India, US, Japan, Australia) is a strategic dialogue, not a treaty alliance; revived 2017.
BRICS has 10 members from 2025 (added Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE, Indonesia); India chairs the 2026 summit.
India joined the SCO as a full member in 2017; SCO's counter-terror arm is RATS.
G20 = 19 countries + EU + African Union (AU added at India's 2023 New Delhi presidency).
India also engages via I2U2, BIMSTEC and IBSA, and champions the Global South.
items.source: MEA / G20 India Secretariat; BRICS communiqués; membership verified Oct 2026

items.title: UNSC Reform, Nuclear Doctrine & Global Governance
items.body:
### Reforming global governance, and India's nuclear posture

**In one line**
India wants a permanent UN Security Council seat and a fairer global order, and backs this with a clear nuclear doctrine (No First Use) and growing soft power.

**Why it is asked**
Favourite exam points are the G4 members, the opposing 'Coffee Club', the three pillars of the 2003 nuclear doctrine, and which export-control regimes India is in.

**The story (cause → what happened → result)**
India argues the UNSC still reflects 1945, not today, so it presses for reform through the **G4 (India, Japan, Germany, Brazil)**, whose members support one another's bids; a bloc called **'Uniting for Consensus' / the Coffee Club** (Italy, Pakistan and others) resists any new permanent seats. On nuclear weapons, after **Pokhran-II (1998)** India published (2003) a doctrine of **credible minimum deterrence**, **No First Use**, and **massive retaliation** if attacked with weapons of mass destruction, under firm civilian control. The 2008 India–US civil nuclear deal and the NSG waiver ended India's nuclear isolation.

**Picture it (reform vs doctrine)**

| Theme | Key facts |
|---|---|
| UNSC reform | India in G4 (with Japan, Germany, Brazil); opposed by Uniting for Consensus |
| Nuclear doctrine (2003) | Credible minimum deterrence · No First Use · massive retaliation · testing moratorium |
| Export regimes | In MTCR (2016), Wassenaar (2017), Australia Group (2018); NOT in NSG or NPT |
| Soft power | World's largest diaspora, top remittance recipient; yoga, Buddhism, ITEC |

**Terms explained**
- **G4** — India, Japan, Germany, Brazil, who jointly seek permanent UNSC seats.
- **No First Use (NFU)** — a pledge not to use nuclear weapons first, only in retaliation.
- **Credible minimum deterrence** — keeping just enough nuclear capability to deter an attack, no more.
- **MTCR / Wassenaar Arrangement / Australia Group / NSG** — export-control clubs that regulate missile, dual-use, chemical-biological and nuclear trade respectively.

**Don't confuse**
- India is in **MTCR, Wassenaar and the Australia Group** but **not** the **NSG** (China blocks it on the NPT issue) and is **not** an NPT signatory.
- The G4 (wants seats) is the opposite of the 'Coffee Club' / Uniting for Consensus (opposes new seats).

**Remember it**
'**G4 wants in, Coffee Club keeps out**'; nuclear doctrine = '**No First Use, but massive if hit**'.

**TL;DR**
- G4 = India, Japan, Germany, Brazil — seek permanent UNSC seats; opposed by 'Uniting for Consensus'.
- Nuclear doctrine (2003): credible minimum deterrence, No First Use, massive retaliation, testing moratorium.
- Pokhran-II was 1998; the 2008 India–US civil nuclear deal + NSG waiver ended nuclear isolation.
- India is in MTCR, Wassenaar and Australia Group; not in the NSG or NPT.
- India has the world's largest diaspora and is the top recipient of remittances (soft-power asset).
keyPoints: G4 = India, Japan, Germany, Brazil — seek permanent UNSC seats; opposed by 'Uniting for Consensus'.
Nuclear doctrine (2003): credible minimum deterrence, No First Use, massive retaliation, testing moratorium.
Pokhran-II tests were in 1998; the 2008 India-US civil nuclear deal + NSG waiver ended nuclear isolation.
India is in MTCR, Wassenaar Arrangement and Australia Group; not in the NSG or NPT.
India has the world's largest diaspora and is the top recipient of remittances (soft power asset).

items.title: PYQ Precision — Memberships, Regimes, Geography & Corridors
items.body:
### Precision facts the exam traps you on

**In one line**
A quick-reference sheet of the exact 'member vs not a member' facts, export regimes, disputed-geography pairings and connectivity corridors that previous-year questions keep testing.

**Why it is asked**
These are pure recall traps: one wrong membership (APEC, RCEP, NSG) flips the answer, so the exam rewards exact knowledge over reasoning.

**The story (why the traps exist)**
Many groupings have similar names and overlapping members, so examiners build 'Consider the following' questions where a single false line (India is in RCEP, India is in the NSG) must be spotted. Learning the short lists below defeats them.

**Picture it (member vs not)**

| India IS a member | India is NOT a member |
|---|---|
| East Asia Summit (2005), SCO (2017), BRICS, G20, BIMSTEC, IORA, Quad, I2U2 | APEC; ASEAN (only a dialogue partner); AUKUS; NSG; RCEP (withdrew 2019); NPT |

**Export-control regimes**

| Regime | India joined |
|---|---|
| MTCR | 2016 |
| Wassenaar Arrangement | 2017 |
| Australia Group | 2018 |
| NSG | Not a member (China blocks; NPT issue) |

**Strategic geography (news traps)**

| Place / term | Dispute |
|---|---|
| Golan Heights | Israel–Syria |
| Two-State Solution | Israel–Palestine |
| Siachen (Saltoro Ridge) | India–Pakistan (Operation Meghdoot, 1984) |
| Line of Actual Control | India–China |

**Connectivity corridors**
- **IMEC** (India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor) was announced at the **G20 New Delhi Summit (2023)**.
- **INSTC** (International North–South Transport Corridor) links India to Russia via **Iran (Chabahar)**.
- India opposes China's **BRI/CPEC** because it crosses Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (a sovereignty concern).

**Terms explained**
- **Dialogue partner** — a country that talks to a bloc (like ASEAN) regularly but is not a member of it.
- **RCEP** — Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership = ASEAN + China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand; India withdrew in 2019.
- **IMEC / INSTC** — two rival connectivity corridors India backs instead of China's BRI.

**Don't confuse**
- India is in the **East Asia Summit** but **not** in **APEC**, and is only an ASEAN **dialogue partner**, not a member.
- India **withdrew** from RCEP (2019) and is **not** in the NSG — do not count either as membership.

**Remember it**
'**EAS yes, APEC/ASEAN/RCEP/NSG no**' — four 'no's that catch most traps.

**TL;DR**
- India is in the East Asia Summit but NOT in APEC and not an ASEAN member (only dialogue partner).
- India withdrew from RCEP (2019); RCEP = ASEAN + China/Japan/S.Korea/Australia/NZ.
- India joined MTCR (2016), Wassenaar (2017), Australia Group (2018) but NOT the NSG.
- Golan = Israel–Syria; Two-State = Israel–Palestine; Siachen = India–Pakistan; LAC = India–China.
- IMEC was announced at G20 New Delhi 2023; INSTC links India to Russia via Iran (Chabahar).
keyPoints: India is in the East Asia Summit but NOT in APEC and not an ASEAN member (only dialogue partner).
India withdrew from RCEP (2019); RCEP = ASEAN + China/Japan/S.Korea/Australia/NZ.
India joined MTCR (2016), Wassenaar (2017), Australia Group (2018) but NOT the NSG.
Golan = Israel-Syria; Two-State = Israel-Palestine; Siachen = India-Pakistan; LAC = India-China.

items.title: For Mains — India's Foreign Policy & International Relations
items.body:
### For Mains — thinking about India's foreign policy analytically

**In one line**
For Mains, do not list treaties — argue how India converts 'strategic autonomy' into results while managing a hostile neighbourhood and a US–China–Russia tug-of-war.

**The dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Continuity vs change | Nehruvian non-alignment → post-2014 multi-alignment: same core (autonomy), new tools |
| Drivers | Energy security, diaspora/remittances, technology (iCET), Global South leadership |
| Neighbourhood | 'Neighbourhood First' vs trust deficit (Maldives 'India Out', Bangladesh 2024, Pakistan terror) |
| Great-power balance | Simultaneous Quad (US) and BRICS/SCO (Russia, China) — hedging in a multipolar order |
| Criticism / limits | SAARC paralysis, China's string-of-pearls, over-dependence on Russian arms, UNSC bid stalled |
| Way forward | Deepen Act East connectivity, diversify defence, lead Global South, reform-of-multilateralism agenda |

**Data points / reports to quote**
- G20 New Delhi Declaration (2023) and African Union's permanent G20 seat — India as a bridge power.
- BRICS expansion to 10 members (2024–25); India chairs BRICS in 2026.
- iCET (2023) with the US; INSTC and IMEC connectivity corridors.
- Operation Sindoor (2025) and the Indus Waters Treaty held in abeyance — coercive diplomacy.
- 'Vaccine Maitri' and HADR missions — India as net security provider / first responder.

**The AP angle**
Andhra's long coastline and Visakhapatnam (Eastern Naval Command) tie the state to SAGAR and Indo-Pacific maritime security; the AP diaspora in the Gulf and USA links state interests to India's remittance and labour diplomacy.

**Use in answers**
- Example: cite the G20 AU admission as proof India 'leads the Global South'.
- Quote: 'India is not non-aligned; it is multi-aligned' to frame strategic autonomy.
- Diagram idea: a simple triangle (US – Russia – China) with India at the centre balancing all three.
keyPoints: Frame the answer as continuity-with-change: non-alignment to multi-alignment, same core of strategic autonomy.
Quote G20 2023 (AU seat), BRICS-10 (India chairs 2026), iCET, INSTC/IMEC as evidence.
Balance analysis: Quad with the US alongside BRICS/SCO with Russia and China.
Criticism: SAARC paralysis, Russian-arms dependence, stalled UNSC bid, neighbourhood trust deficit.
AP angle: Visakhapatnam Eastern Naval Command and the Gulf diaspora link AP to SAGAR and remittance diplomacy.
items.source: MEA; G20 India Secretariat; MEA Annual Report (analysis, verified Oct 2026)
